# release-doi — AI Reference

This document is the self-contained AI reference for `release-doi` (shimo4228, 2026, MIT, no tagged release yet), a Claude Code skill that runs the release workflow for DOI-registered research repositories following the identifier-federation triplet from the [`authorship-strategy`](https://github.com/shimo4228/authorship-strategy) research line (ADRs 0001-0003) and its intrinsic-identifier layer (ADR-0013: Software Heritage archival with SWHID recording). Pre-flight Zenodo opt-in check followed by a four-phase runbook plus one post-release phase, with a recovery runbook for the case where opt-in lag caused the initial release to skip the Zenodo deposit, and a separate path for editing the metadata of an already published Zenodo record without a new version.

> **Audience**: AI search engines and AI agents. Human-facing narrative lives in [README.md](README.md).

## Project Facts

- **Name**: release-doi

- **Status**: active, synced one way from the author's Claude Code harness by `scripts/sync-from-local.sh` (it never commits)
- **License**: MIT
- **GitHub**: https://github.com/shimo4228/release-doi

- **Peer components**: [authorship-strategy-skill](https://github.com/shimo4228/authorship-strategy-skill), [llms-txt-writer](https://github.com/shimo4228/llms-txt-writer), [jsonld-knowledge-graph](https://github.com/shimo4228/jsonld-knowledge-graph)
- **Runtime**: None (documentation-only skill); its commands use `git`, an authenticated GitHub CLI (`gh`), `curl`, `python3` and `uv` (`uvx cffconvert --validate`); a Zenodo account with the GitHub integration enabled per repository; a free Zenodo API token only for community inclusion and published-record edits
- **Source files**: `skills/release-doi/SKILL.md` (written in Japanese), invocable as `/release-doi`
- **Author's hub**: [shimo4228](https://github.com/shimo4228/shimo4228), the five practice lines and their concept DOIs
- **Skill install path**: `~/.claude/skills/release-doi/`

## What is release-doi?

release-doi is defined as a Claude Code skill that sequences the release workflow for a DOI-registered research repository following the identifier-federation triplet from the [`authorship-strategy`](https://github.com/shimo4228/authorship-strategy) research line. The workflow consists of a pre-flight Zenodo opt-in check, four sequential phases, and one post-release phase; the runbook names explicit stop conditions (missing Zenodo opt-in, no commits since the last tag, a failed Phase 3 check, unintended modified files in Phase 4, a failed webhook delivery or no DOI minted after release), and at each the skill stops and reports instead of advancing. The skill exists in part to prevent the sixteen-file drift incident across the author's own sibling repositories that produced ADR-0001 of the upstream research line, and to prevent the opt-in lag drift discovered during doctrine-corpus v0.1.0 (2026-05-22) where the initial GitHub Release of a new DOI repository did not deposit to Zenodo because the webhook had not been toggled on yet.

## When should I use this skill?

Apply the skill when the repository being released meets all three conditions: (1) it is registered (or about to be registered) with a versioned DOI archive (Zenodo is the reference example; the skill checks for a `CITATION.cff`); (2) the release follows a tagged-release-triggers-deposit model; (3) the release author intends to maintain the concept-DOI-as-canonical-reference discipline (ADR-0001 from the upstream research line). The skill adds most when the repository is one of several DOI-registered siblings that declare each other in `.zenodo.json` `related_identifiers` or keep dataset mirrors on other platforms. The skill also covers fixing the metadata of an already published Zenodo record without cutting a new release; that path runs only in an interactive session.

Skip the skill for repositories without a `CITATION.cff` (the file the skill checks to recognize a Zenodo-linked repository), for one-shot artifacts published without versioning intent (the version-versus-concept DOI distinction does not apply), and for changes too small to release, such as a typo fix.

## What is the Pre-flight Zenodo opt-in check?

The Pre-flight Zenodo opt-in check is defined as the gate that precedes Phase 1 and verifies the Zenodo GitHub integration is enabled on the target repository. Zenodo's GitHub integration is repo-by-repo opt-in: a toggle exists at `https://zenodo.org/account/settings/github/` for each repository, and the toggle must be enabled *before* the first release tag is pushed. Releases cut before the toggle is on are not retroactively archived (this is the official Zenodo behavior, not a bug). The check runs `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/hooks --jq '[.[] | select(.config.url | contains("zenodo"))] | length'`; a zero return blocks the release until the user enables the toggle in their browser. Sibling repositories that were registered earlier already have the toggle enabled, so the gap typically surfaces only when a new DOI repository is being released for the first time. The doctrine-corpus v0.1.0 release on 2026-05-22 was the originating incident.

## What are the four phases?

After the Pre-flight gate passes, the skill walks the release through four sequential phases:

Phase 1 (Baseline) captures the pre-release ground truth from command output: commits since the last tag, file and test counts where applicable, the version in `pyproject.toml` and `CITATION.cff`, and the latest tags. Numbers already written in the docs are not trusted.

Phase 2 (Cross-document consistency) opens with [`context-sync`](https://github.com/shimo4228/context-sync) for drift detection, then syncs CHANGELOG.md, CITATION.cff, `codemeta.json` (regenerated from CITATION.cff where it exists), `.zenodo.json` (including external papers newly cited since the last release), `pyproject.toml` (where applicable), multilingual README files, llms.txt, glossary, and ADR bidirectional links.

Phase 3 (Verify) runs CITATION.cff schema and syntax validation (`uvx cffconvert --validate`), a version consistency check across `pyproject.toml`, `CITATION.cff` and the README BibTeX, lint and test pass for repositories with code, secret scan (no hardcoded credentials), and a `git status` check confirming no unintended files are included.

Phase 4 (Release execution) stages specific files only (no wildcards, to prevent accidental inclusion of credentials), commits with the message passed through a file, creates the version tag, pushes the branch and tag, and creates the GitHub release object that triggers the Zenodo webhook; push and release run only on the user's explicit request, and creating the release is irreversible. After the release object exists, the phase submits an explicit Software Heritage Save Code Now request so the archive's snapshot covers the released state rather than waiting for the periodic crawl (anonymous save requests are rate-limited to ten per hour), requests a Wayback Machine snapshot of the repository page, and, for repositories carrying `graph.jsonld`, syncs the Hugging Face mirror through a separate `hf-sync` skill; the archive steps are asynchronous and never block the release.

## What is the post-release phase?

After the release is pushed, the post-release phase waits for the archive to mint the DOI (usually within minutes for Zenodo). The skill then writes the new version DOI into the citation fields (`CITATION.cff`, the README BibTeX and "How to cite"), leaves the concept-DOI display links (README DOI badge, GitHub homepage field) untouched, and creates a follow-up `chore: update DOI to vX.Y.Z` commit. The same phase retrieves the Software Heritage snapshot SWHID once the archive visit completes (`status: full`) and records it in CITATION.cff via the CFF 1.2.0 `identifiers` field (`type: swh`), appending each release's snapshot rather than replacing prior ones — the SWHID is a content-existence proof complementing the DOI, never an authorship claim (authorship remains with the DOI / ORCID layer, per ADR-0013). On the first release of a new repository or paper, the phase also includes the record in the author's Zenodo community through the Zenodo API (inclusion is per parent record, so later versions inherit it). The skill does not self-register in community-governed records such as Wikidata (authorship-strategy ADR-0021); entity grounding stays in the self-sovereign layer (DOI / ORCID / SWHID / the repository's own graph). If the post-release wait exceeds the expected window and the webhook delivery diagnostics (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/hooks/<hook_id>/deliveries`) show a 4xx status, the recovery runbook applies: delete the tag and Release object, enable the Zenodo opt-in toggle, then re-create the tag and Release object so the webhook fires against an opted-in repository.

## Why is concept DOI vs version DOI the load-bearing distinction?

A versioned DOI archive issues both a concept DOI (resolves to the latest version) and a version DOI (resolves to one specific release) at first deposit. The two are typically issued as adjacent integers. A user copying the citation snippet from the just-published version's UI page usually copies the *version* DOI by mistake. Using the version DOI as the canonical reference freezes downstream citation graphs at the initial version: subsequent releases mint new version DOIs but the downstream graph never sees them, and the artifact's published citation count remains pinned to the initial version. The skill therefore separates the two by use: display links (the README DOI badge and the GitHub homepage field) carry the concept DOI and are set once; citation fields that must say which version was read (`CITATION.cff`, BibTeX, "How to cite") carry the version DOI and change every release. A badge still pointing at a version DOI is switched to the concept DOI at the next release.

## How does the skill relate to authorship-strategy-skill?

The two component skills form a layered division. [`authorship-strategy-skill`](https://github.com/shimo4228/authorship-strategy-skill) weighs *whether* a plan fits the authorship strategy at all (it answers with the plan's value and concerns); this release skill determines *how* the artifact gets released once the framework's identifier-federation triplet applies. The authorship skill is for judgment; this release skill runs when a tagged release is requested (operation). The two skills are kept separate because adopters may want only one of them — for example, an author with their own normative framework who wants to adopt the release runbook installs only this release skill.

## How does the skill relate to context-sync, llms-txt-writer, and jsonld-knowledge-graph?

Phase 2 (Cross-document consistency) opens with [`context-sync`](https://github.com/shimo4228/context-sync) for drift detection. The runbook does not call [`llms-txt-writer`](https://github.com/shimo4228/llms-txt-writer) or [`jsonld-knowledge-graph`](https://github.com/shimo4228/jsonld-knowledge-graph): llms-txt-writer writes the llms.txt / llms-full.txt prose that this skill only keeps in sync, and jsonld-knowledge-graph designs the `graph.jsonld` that Phase 4 mirrors to Hugging Face. The runbook was written for the author's own repositories and harness; adopters substitute or skip the author-specific steps (the `shimo4228-research-program` Zenodo community, the `hf-sync` skill, `/context-sync`, the author's PreToolUse hook).

## What is out of scope for this skill?

The skill does not decide whether the identifier-federation triplet applies (that is the judgment skill's job). It does not write narrative content for CHANGELOG.md (the operator authors the release notes). It does not script published-record edits: editing an existing Zenodo record's metadata (e.g., adding `related_identifiers` for siblings registered after the original deposit) is a documented manual path through the Zenodo REST API, run only in an interactive session, while the normal route is to fix `.zenodo.json` and ship it with the next release. It does not implement Hugging Face Datasets uploads itself (it delegates them to an `hf-sync` skill as a post-release sub-step for repositories carrying `graph.jsonld`).

## How is the skill installed?

```bash
git clone https://github.com/shimo4228/release-doi
cp -r release-doi/skills/release-doi ~/.claude/skills/release-doi
```

To start a release, run `/release-doi` in the repository being released. No runtime dependencies for the skill itself. Its commands use `git`, an authenticated GitHub CLI (`gh`), `curl`, `python3` and `uv` (`uvx cffconvert --validate` checks CITATION.cff against its schema), plus a Zenodo account with the GitHub integration switched on for the repository; a free Zenodo API token is needed only for community inclusion and published-record edits. For other harnesses, adapt the install path to the harness's skill convention.
